explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Luke 15:2 says the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble. Tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus, and these two groups looked at that crowd and started muttering. Nobody asked them for a review, but they gave one anyway.

Not the disciples, friend. The text says the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble (Luke 15:2). The disciples aren't mentioned in this scene at all. Jesus' own followers get the benefit of the doubt here, because the text never has them complaining.

No soldiers in this scene, friend. Luke 15:1 mentions tax collectors and sinners gathering around to listen to Jesus, and then Luke 15:2 says the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble. The Romans never show up in these verses. The complaining comes from people standing close enough to watch.

explanations.answer: He welcomes sinners and eats with them
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The Pharisees and scribes say, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” (Luke 15:2) They meant it as a complaint. Jesus is about to answer it with a parable, and I'm telling you, it's a good one.

explanations.answer: He heals people on the Sabbath day
explanations.explanation: That complaint is real in other places, friend, but it isn't the one here. In Luke 15:2 the grumbling is about who Jesus welcomes and who He eats with. Healing doesn't come up at all in this passage. Right complaint, wrong chapter.

explanations.answer: He doesn't wash before He eats
explanations.explanation: Close to the table, but not the complaint here. The grumbling in Luke 15:2 is about the company: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” Hand washing never comes up in these verses. Their problem is the guest list.

explanations.answer: Leaves the ninety-nine and goes after it
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Jesus says the man does “leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it” (Luke 15:4). He doesn't stop at a quick look, either. He keeps going until he finds it.

explanations.answer: Stays put and guards the ninety-nine
explanations.explanation: Reasonable plan, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He asks, “What man among you… does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?” (Luke 15:4) The man goes after the one that is lost. I think the ninety-nine are in for a very quiet afternoon.

explanations.answer: Sends a servant out to look for it
explanations.explanation: No servant in this story, friend. Jesus says the man himself leaves the ninety-nine in the pasture and goes after the one that is lost (Luke 15:4). He goes personally, and he doesn't turn back until he finds it.
True. Luke 15:5 says that when he finds it, “he joyfully puts it on his shoulders.” Joyfully, friend. The text says the man is happy about this.

It's actually true, friend. Luke 15:5 says, “he joyfully puts it on his shoulders.” The man finds the sheep, and his first move is to pick it up with joy. The text says nothing about scolding or dragging.

explanations.answer: Calls his friends and neighbors to rejoice
explanations.explanation: Yes! He “comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!’” (Luke 15:6) He finds the sheep and he wants everybody to know. I'd have posted the news before I got home.

explanations.answer: Builds a stronger pen for the whole flock
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the text doesn't have him building anything. After he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!” (Luke 15:6) The next thing in the story is the celebration.

explanations.answer: Counts all hundred sheep one more time
explanations.explanation: Nice instinct, but Jesus doesn't say that. In Luke 15:6 the man comes home and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!” He's busy celebrating.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.” (Luke 15:7) The joy is bigger over the one who repents. That's the surprise in the parable.

False is right. Luke 15:7 says, “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.” The one sinner who repents gets the bigger joy. Jesus said it plainly, and I'll take Him at His word.

explanations.answer: Lights a lamp and sweeps her house
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says she does “light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it” (Luke 15:8). Lamp, broom and a careful search. She doesn't quit early.

explanations.answer: Asks her neighbors to help her look
explanations.explanation: Not at this point, friend. Luke 15:8 says she lights a lamp, sweeps her house, and searches carefully until she finds it. The neighbors come into the story later, after she finds the coin, when she calls them together to rejoice (Luke 15:9).

explanations.answer: Waits for it to turn up on its own
explanations.explanation: She's not the waiting type, friend. Jesus says she does “light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it.” (Luke 15:8) She goes after that coin herself, and she doesn't stop until she finds it.
